Vs.

full_judgment:
After the institution of the suit, the plaintiff petitioner filed an application for injunction restraining the principal defendants from leasing out the Waqf portion of the Ahsangonj Hat with any other person and also from interfering in any way of its possession and management of the said hat till the disposal of the suit. In the application the petitioner stated that the Waqf Estate has the right to hold the waqf portion of the Ahsangonj Hat which has not been vested in the Government either under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or under any other law, that no compensation or annuity of the hat has been assessed or paid by the Government, to the Waqf Estate and the Government never exercised any act of possession over the said hat at any point of time, that the income of the hat is utilised for which the Waqf Estate was created and that if possession of the hat is taken over from the plaintiff, it would suffer irreparable loss and injury. 

 3. Defendant-opposite Party No. 1 filed written objection against the prayer for temporary injunction. Their case is that the plaintiff was the owner of the hat in question. The Ahsangonj tahsil office is situated in the middle of the said hat. Out of the land of the Waqf Estate, an area measuring 3.69 acres of land of Khatian No. 322 are not retainable land under the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The management of the said hat was given to the Mutawalli as per lease granted by the Government vide order No. VIII 376/73(1) 125 ME dated 10-2-1975 and 1382 BS and in pursuance of such order of lease, the mutawalli of the Waqf Estate managed -the suit hat for the period between 10-2-1980 and 2-12-1982. Subsequently by Memo No. SLV/114/78/629(83) dated 2-11-1978 of the Ministry of LGRD, the possession of the said hat was taken overlong before the filing of the suit and the plaintiff was also intimated about the fact. The Waqf Estate is entitled to annuity of the said hat as admissible under the law through the Waqf Administrator. The management of the hat in question has been given in favour of Ahsangonj Union Parishad and the same was sold in auction for the last 5 months and the Government realised rent of Taka 1,25,000 and therefore, the prayer for injunction is not legally maintainable. 

 6. Mr Sk Afzalur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the Waqf Estate is entitled to retain the suit hat and section 10A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the case, inasmuch as, the land comprising Waqf Estate is one of waqf-lillah, not a Waqf-ul-Aulad as the purpose for creating waqf was for the interest and benefit of the religious institutions. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned Subordinate Judge considering that aspect of the matter granted temporary injunction in favour of the petitioner and the Court of appeal below without properly considering that aspect of the matter illegally vacated the order of injunction and thereby has committed an error of law which has occasioned failure of justice. 

 7. Mr Abdul Quaiyum, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, on the other hand, submits that on a plain reading of the plaint, the relief claimed therein is barred under section 72 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and therefore, the plaintiff is not entitled to any order of injunction. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further submits that the hat in question was taken over by the Government and thereafter the Waqf Estate took lease from the Government and then it was again taken over by the Government and placed under the management of the local Union Parishad and therefore, the learned Additional District Judge has committed no error of law in vacating the order of injunction. 

 8. Admittedly, the suit property is a hat. In the plaint which was produced at the time of hearing the Rule, I have noticed that there is no averment therein that no annuity has been fixed by the Government but in the application for injunction, it has been stated that no annuity has been fixed by the Government. The specific case of the Government is that annuity has been fixed in respect of the suit property and Government has taken over possession of the suit hat and the management of the hat has been given to Ahsangonj Union Parishad. The further claim of the government is that the hat in question was leased out in favour of the Waqf Estate and thereafter the Waqf Estate instituted various writ petitions and suits and continued in possession for sometime on the strength of stay order. It has been further asserted by the Government that after vacating the stay orders, the government took over possession from the Waqf Estate with the assistance of a Magistrate. As regards institution of Writ Petition and suits, relating to the suit hat, there is admission in the plaint itself. The suit property being hat is not retain able land under section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 9. The petitioner Waqf Estate has not set up any case claiming benefit of section 10A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned Advocate rather submits that section 10A is not applicable. This is a confused submission, inasmuch as, the plaintiff cannot claim any right, other than a right under section 10A, if there be any, in the suit land after the acquisition of the rent receiving interest by the Government. This provision provides that where the rent receiving interests of a Waqf property, any Debuttar or other religious trusts, had been acquired under sub- section (1) or (2) of section 3, but the Government has not exercised its right of possession over such interest, the Mutawalli, Shebaits or Trustees, as the case may be, holding such interest on the date of acquisition, shall continue and be deemed to have continued such interest as agent of the Government till the last day of the agricultural year in which the final publication of the compensation assessment roll under sub-section (2) of section 43 or till the time the Government exercises right of possession over such interest. As the plaintiff-petitioner has not set up any claim as above, the suit is apparently not maintainable. 

 10. The learned Additional District Judge observed that from the petition filed by the Mutawalli to the Minister, Ministry of LGRD., the plaintiff has admitted that the annuity of the suit property has been fixed at Taka 2000 for 5 years. I find sufficient materials on record in support of the observation made by the learned Additional District Judge. On the other hand, the learned Subordinate Judge held that there would be setback in the management of the Waqf Estate if the suit property is taken over by the Government without fixing the annuity. This finding is not based upon proper consideration of the materials on record. As observed above, the suit was not filed setting up any case claiming benefit of section 10A. The suit was instituted seeking declaration that the plaintiff has the right to hold the suit property which is admittedly non-retainable land. Therefore, I am of the view that the suit is hit by section 72 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 13. The learned Additional District Judge while rejecting the prayer for injunction came to the finding that the suit hat has been recorded in the name of Government as Ahsangonj hat both in the SA record as well as in the RS Khatian and that the plaintiff Waqf Estate did not take any step against the said record of right. The learned Additional District Judge further held that the claim of the plaintiff that the Waqf Estate is in its possession is not a believable one. This finding of prima facie possession, in my view, is based upon proper consideration of the materials on record. The plaintiff-petitioner admitted in the plaint that it took lease of the suit hat from the government. Therefore, the learned Additional District Judge has rightly held that the government has taken over possession of the suit hat. In the premises, ram of the view that the balance of convenience and inconvenience is against the plaintiff and is in favour of the defendant Government. 

 14. Though Mr Sk Afzalur Rahman strenuously submits that the Waqf Estate is in possession and it can retain possession till the disposal of the suit otherwise the very purpose for which the Waqf Estate was created will be frustrated, but he failed to substantiate his claim. How the plaintiff can retain its alleged possession if the law does not permit the petitioner to retain possession of non-retainable land. He has also failed to satisfy me that the observation of the Court of appeal below that the Government has taken over possession of the Waqf Estate prior to the filing of the suit are based upon no materials on record. The Court of appeal below on proper consideration of the materials on record has come to the conclusion that the plaintiff has failed its prima facie possession in the suit hat and has rightly interfered with the order of the learned Subordinate Judge. I do not find any illegality or impropriety in the order of the Court of appeal below. 

 15. Mr Sk Afzalur Rahman has referred a decision in the case of Province of East Pakistan and another vs Md Mehedi Ali Khan and others, 11 DLR (SC) 318. The said decision has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the case. Mr Afzalur Rahman made confused submissions without properly appreciating sections lOA, 20 and 72 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Section 10A came into force on 24-5-1960 by section 2 of Ordinance No. IX of 1960. This is a special provision in favour of a Mutawalli of Waqf Estate regarding collection of rent due from a Waqf property. This provision is a temporary measure which will last in case of rent receiving interest from the date of its acquisition provided the Government has not started collecting rent. In this case, I have noticed that the Government has already exercised its right by collecting rent and the plaintiff has also taken lease from the Government. I therefore, find no substance in the submission of the learned Advocate. The plaintiff-petitioner is not entitled to an order of injunction both on facts as well as on law. Accordingly, I find no substance in this Rule.
